title: By the charcoal fire (John 18:12–27)
hook: Peter warms himself and denies him

segments.voice: Yesterday, torches in the garden, Malchus's ear, and two words that knocked soldiers to the ground. Your line: I am he.

Two scenes are happening at once tonight, and John cuts between them like a film editor. Inside, Jesus is questioned by Annas, father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas. Outside, in the courtyard, it's cold. Servants and officers have built a fire, hands out to the warmth. And among them stands Peter. Earlier tonight he said he would lay down his life for Jesus. Then he swung a sword in the garden. Now he's at a fire, trying to look like he belongs.

In the King James Bible: "And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves: and Peter stood with them, and warmed himself." Three times, Peter is asked. First the girl who keeps the door: "Art not thou also one of this man's disciples? He saith, I am not." Then someone at the fire asks the same, and again: I am not. Then a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter cut off: "Did not I see thee in the garden with him?" Peter denied again, "and immediately the cock crew." Put this beside yesterday. In the garden, Jesus said, ego eimi, I am. At the fire, Peter says, ouk eimi, I am not. John sets them almost side by side. One steps forward; one steps back into the crowd. And inside, at the same time, Jesus tells the high priest: I spoke openly to the world; ask the people who heard me. He's naming witnesses, while one of his own disciples stands outside saying he isn't one. One more detail. The Greek word for this charcoal fire is anthrakia. John will use that word for a fire once more, much later. Hold on to it. Readers have long found Peter's denial painful and strangely hopeful at once. Painful because it's so ordinary: he isn't tortured, just asked by a doorkeeper. Hopeful because the church remembers this same Peter, later on, as a leader.
screen: `A FIRE OF COALS, FOR IT WAS COLD.`
`I AM, INSIDE; I AM NOT, OUTSIDE.`
then, large: `AND PETER STOOD WITH THEM, AND WARMED HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Peter's fire was a comfort and a hiding place at once, so think gently about yours: the group you go along with, the joke you laugh at to fit in, the silence you keep when someone you love isn't there to defend themselves. Don't scold yourself; just notice where you stand to stay warm. If you pray, bring that place to God honestly; if not, simply name it to yourself.
Anthrakia. The Greek word for the charcoal fire where Peter warmed himself and said, three times, I am not.
Your line: warming himself. Peter's story isn't over yet, not by a long way. The fire will be back.

howItsDone: Peter's denial is read in churches during Holy Week, and in Christian art a rooster beside Peter recalls it, a reminder both of failure and of forgiveness.

what a scholar hears: ego eimi in the garden and ouk eimi at the fire, and anthrakia, a word John uses here and again at 21:9.

chat.says: Peter denied Jesus three times? What was so scary that night?
options: Nothing dramatic. A doorkeeper asked him, and he said, I am not.
Soldiers tortured him at the fire until he said he never knew Jesus.
Malchus himself found him and threatened him with the same sword.
chat.meaning: He wasn't tortured, just asked by a doorkeeper and others at the fire. While Jesus said I am inside, Peter said I am not.

Annas.meaning: father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas

notes: anthrakia occurs only in John 18:18 and 21:9 in the NT. Confirm.
'Annas, the old high priest': John calls him father-in-law of Caiaphas (18:13); Annas had been high priest earlier. Confirm.
Rooster on steeples as a reminder of Peter's denial: a common explanation, though weathercock origins are debated. Confirm or cut from howItsDone.
The day avoids teaching day 654's breakfast scene; it only notes the word returns.
